schools.summary: Barnes explains the "upper coasts" as the interior table-land against low-lying Ephesus; Ellicott traces the inland route; Robertson identifies the Cayster road, describes Asia and Ephesus, and denies any link between these disciples and Apollos.
Gill sets Apollos at Corinth and the party formed in his name; Calvin sees the church confirmed by a miracle and holds the twelve to have been Jews, since they had John's baptism.
Henry contrasts Paul planting at Ephesus with Apollos watering at Corinth, and places the twelve in the lowest form of Christ's school under John the Baptist.
Clarke reports the Codex Bezae opening and lists the inland provinces; Wesley gives the geography and calls the disciples imperfectly instructed followers of the Baptist.

debates.question: Who were the twelve disciples Paul found at Ephesus?

sides.position: converts of Apollos, or men of exactly his standing before he was better taught
unconnected followers of the Baptist who had drifted into Ephesus

themes: Ephesus and the temple of Diana

schools.summary: Barnes distinguishes ordinary converting grace from the miraculous gifts and reads the answer sympathetically; Ellicott re-translates "when ye believed" and diagnoses a want of spiritual gifts and joy; Robertson notes the interrogative idiom and Paul's suspicion.
Gill limits the question to the extraordinary gifts; Calvin argues that Jews could not have been ignorant of the Spirit as such, so a figure of speech must be at work.

Clarke insists they cannot have meant they never heard of the Spirit, since John announced the coming baptizer, and guesses they were Asiatic Jews baptized at Jerusalem long before; Wesley reads the question of the extraordinary gifts.

Barnes takes the question as asking what doctrine they professed; Robertson renders it "on what basis" and notes this as the last mention of John the Baptist in the New Testament; Ellicott treats the exchange as a completed diagnosis of their position.
Gill sets out the two senses of the question — in whose name they were baptized, and what attended the baptism.
Wesley opens the question into two: into what dispensation, and to the sealing of what doctrine?

themes: the last mention of the Baptist

schools.summary: Barnes gives the design of John's coming as preparation for the Messiah; Ellicott treats the verse as a summary of fuller teaching and finds the elementary doctrines of Hebrews behind it; Robertson takes the genitive as descriptive, not instrumental, and denies that Paul calls John's baptism inadequate.
Gill argues that John's baptism was in substance the same as Christ's; Calvin turns the verse into a summons forward, since the sense of want is what makes a man desire what he lacks.
Clarke isolates what was peculiar to John — the direction to believe on the coming one; Wesley notes that John here gives way to Christ altogether.

Barnes argues on four grounds that this was a second baptism, concludes that John's baptism was not strictly Christian, and denies that anything here licenses repeating Christian baptism; Robertson holds these men were not so much baptized again as really baptized this time.
Gill identifies the hearers of the first clause; Calvin denies that water baptism was repeated at all, taking Luke to speak of a baptism with the Spirit, as elsewhere.
Clarke accepts a second baptism here and warns in the strongest terms against iterating a baptism already essentially performed; Wesley says they were baptized twice but not with the same baptism.

debates.question: Was a second baptism in water administered here?

sides.position: yes — these men had never been baptized as Christ prescribed
no — Luke speaks of their being baptized with the Spirit, the laying on of hands being added by way of explanation

debates.question: Does the verse license repeating Christian baptism?

sides.position: no — there is no command and no example, and to iterate a valid baptism is a grave wrong

themes: in the name of the Lord Jesus

schools.summary: Robertson sets the laying on of hands beside Samaria and Damascus, reads both verbs as inchoative imperfects, and denies that the water conveyed the Spirit; Ellicott corrects the tense to continuous action and argues that tongues meant ecstatic praise rather than foreign languages.
Gill draws the parallel with Peter and John laying hands on the Samaritans already baptized by Philip.
Henry marks the suddenness of the change and passes on the suggestion that the gifts fitted these men for the ministry.
Clarke takes the tongues as the miraculous gift of foreign languages, used to teach the doctrines of Christianity.

debates.question: What was the gift of tongues here?

sides.position: the power of speaking foreign languages, used for teaching
an ecstatic and jubilant praise, of which foreign speech is too small an account

themes: the Spirit not conveyed by water

schools.summary: Ellicott re-orders the English so the number covers the whole group, and suggests the twelve were living together as a kind of ascetic community.
Gill notes the versions that drop the qualifying word, and takes these men for the first materials of the Ephesian church, very likely its elders.
Henry reports the same conjecture about the elders.

themes: the first materials of a church

fidelity.note: the closing sentence, weighing the number against what these men had just confessed not to know, is the summary's own framing; the facts in it are Luke's and the conjecture about the elders is Gill's and Henry's

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson read the participles as conative; Robertson notes the three months without interruption and equates the kingdom with the church purchased with Christ's blood; Ellicott reckons up the labour of those months, tent-making and synagogue preaching together.
Gill notes the sabbath custom and Paul's affection for his countrymen; Calvin defines the kingdom as free forgiveness and newness of life, and pairs sound reasoning with godly exhortation.
Henry analyses the preaching as argumentative, affectionate and undaunted, and calls three months a competent time for consideration.
Clarke states the rule that Paul always offered salvation to the Jews first.
Chrysostom sees Paul forcing his way into the synagogue everywhere so that the break should come from the Jews' side, and denies that his boldness was harshness.

Ellicott and Robertson read the hardening as progressive and identify "the Way" as a name for the movement; Robertson describes the withdrawal as a cleavage and the founding of a separate church; Barnes objects to "disputing" as a rendering and defends separation as prudence.
Gill states the double effect of the word as a savour of life and of death; Calvin makes the withdrawal a rule of patience exhausted and commends Paul's daily diligence.
Clarke identifies Tyrannus as a Jewish schoolmaster who lent his room and rejects the reading that makes the name a title; Wesley notes the teaching was now daily, not weekly.

sides.position: a Jewish teacher who lent or let his room
a benefactor who built the school and gave it to the city
a physician of a family known from an Ephesian inscription, possibly known to Luke

schools.summary: Robertson reconciles the two years with the three of the farewell speech, traces the spread of the gospel over the province and Paul's Corinthian anxieties in these years, and cites Pliny; Ellicott makes Ephesus the centre from which the other churches of the Revelation sprang; Barnes explains the influx into the city.
Gill dates the two years from the end of the three months; Calvin denies that anyone had to travel, the word being carried hand to hand by every man for himself.
Clarke supposes Paul journeyed through the towns and villages himself and takes the Greeks for the heathen at large; Wesley notes that the ban on preaching in Asia had now expired.

themes: the word carried hand to hand

schools.summary: Ellicott shows the phrase is negative and identifies the noun as the physicians' word for healing virtues; Robertson calls it litotes, notes the imperfect, and explains why such proofs were needed against Ephesian magic; Barnes finds the same idiom in Longinus.
Gill distinguishes these from common miracles and makes God the efficient cause; Calvin reads "by the hand of" as ascribing the praise to God alone.
Clarke renders them miracles of no ordinary kind; Wesley says they were wrought in a very uncommon manner.

Barnes identifies both Latin words and denies any virtue in the cloths, treating them as a sign only; Ellicott asks why Luke dwells on the detail, allows the medium a real function in strengthening faith, and extends the principle to relics; Robertson answers that the power is in God, who condescends to meet ignorance where he can reach it.

Gill gives the domestic sense of the handkerchief and the workman's apron; Calvin insists Paul chose the meanest objects precisely so that no superstition should arise, and refuses the passage to the defenders of relics.
Clarke marks the evident distinction between the diseases and the evil spirits; Wesley allows that the spirits caused many diseases that looked natural.

debates.question: What accounts for the healing power of the cloths?

sides.position: nothing in the objects; they were a sign of whose instrumentality the cure came by
a real function as a medium strengthening faith, on which footing cures ascribed to relics admit a like explanation
no power in superstition at all, but God condescending to weak faith
the meanness of the objects was chosen against superstition, and the passage gives relics no support

schools.summary: Barnes rescues the word "vagabond" and explains the title exorcist from the oath used; Robertson compares travelling fortune-tellers, notes the article before the name as a magic formula, and the assumption that success turned on exactness; Ellicott places them below Simon and Elymas and says the Name was to them one more formula.
Gill describes the trade; Calvin traces the office itself to a foolish emulation of the prophets and finds two faults in the invocation — colour without faith, and a calling nobody gave them.
Henry works out what such men could claim whichever way the experiment went, and notes their formula named the preacher rather than any faith of their own.
Clarke gives the commercial motive in a city full of demoniacs; Wesley calls it a vain undertaking, since Satan yields to nothing but faith.
Chrysostom says they did everything by way of trade, having no mind to believe.

Barnes rules out the high priesthood and reads the title of the priestly order; Ellicott suggests the title was itself part of the imposture; Robertson admits ignorance, notes the variant reading, and reads the seven sons as a judgement on Ephesian Judaism.
Henry grieves that the house of Aaron should be found in league with Satan and supposes a rambling humour turned them into mountebanks.
Clarke prefers the Codex Bezae reading and quotes Josephus on Eleazar's exorcism before Vespasian, judging the ring and the cup plain imposture.

debates.question: In what sense was Sceva a chief priest?

sides.position: of the priestly order, a priest of distinction, not the high priest
head of one of the twenty-four courses, taken at face value
the title was part of the imposture, a name he gave himself
simply "a certain priest", following the Codex Bezae

schools.summary: Ellicott and Robertson distinguish the two verbs — recognition of authority against familiar acquaintance — and Robertson notes the emphatic word order of the closing question; Barnes puts the reply in terms of jurisdiction.
Gill notes the versions that add "to them", fixing the retort on the seven.
Henry hears the answer as extorted by the power of God to shame those who misused the Name, and turns it against every faction that professes zeal while serving its own interest.
Clarke renders the two verbs distinctly and cites an old English Bible that kept the difference.

themes: Jesus I know, and Paul I know

schools.summary: Robertson gives the verbs their force — springing like a panther, mastering — and shows that "both" covers all seven; Ellicott compares the strength of the Gadarene, reads "naked" of the outer cloak only, and finds in the story's abrupt end a mark of truthfulness; Barnes cites parallel instances of such strength.
Calvin explains why the act is attributed to the man, and reads God's purpose as showing that his power is not contained in the sound of a voice.
Henry makes the scene a warning to all who name Christ's name without departing from iniquity.
Clarke turns the disparity of numbers into an argument for the spirit's presence.

themes: a name used as a charm

schools.summary: Robertson notes the imperfect and calls it a notable victory over the powers of evil; Barnes reads the failure of the impostors as evidence distinguishing them from Paul; Ellicott states the lesson the city drew about using the Name without faith.
Gill supposes spectators enough to spread the story; Calvin sees a purpose in the publicity, that the name of Christ should reach more men.
Henry separates the two effects — terror at what they had seen, and glory to a name now shown to be above every name — and warns against compounding Christ's religion with paganism.
Clarke follows exorcism forward into the practice of the early church; Wesley notes that the malice of the devil here furthered the gospel.

Robertson reads the imperfect as a stream of penitents and is candid that believers had kept secret occult contacts; Ellicott corrects the translation, thinks the confession public, and describes the conscience roused by contact with the unseen; Barnes makes willingness to confess a test of renewal.
Calvin values the confession because it was voluntary, refuses to build a general law on it, and distinguishes it point by point from auricular confession.
Wesley credits the free and open confession to the word penetrating the inmost soul.

Barnes and Ellicott assemble the ancient evidence for the Ephesian letters, Ellicott tracing them to an older Phrygian nature-worship and explaining the burning as the cure of a superstition treated homoeopathically; Robertson gives the trade sense of the word and cites Deissmann on the magical papyri.
Calvin widens the term to cover astrology and every divination about the future, and reads the price as proof that the faithful despised gain.
Henry lists the motives for burning rather than keeping the books — indignation, resolution, the removal of temptation, and the prevention of mischief to others.
Clarke retails Suidas and Hesychius on the six words, and computes the sum several ways; Wesley holds burning better than selling, even for the poor's sake.

debates.question: What was the fifty thousand pieces of silver worth?

sides.position: Attic drachmae, some £1,770, worth much more in purchasing power
sestertii or denarii, between £400 and £1,600
roughly two thousand pounds
Jewish shekels, over six thousand pounds

schools.summary: Robertson explains the military phrase and the two imperfects; Ellicott notes the continuous growth and the better reading; Barnes turns the episode into a settled principle about withdrawing property from a dishonest trade rather than selling it on.
Gill lists what the word had prevailed over and reports a variant reading about faith; Calvin divides the two verbs between numbers added and believers deepened.
Henry describes what extensive growth and inward prevailing each look like.
Clarke reports the Codex Bezae addition and dates Paul's fighting with beasts to this period; Wesley divides the verbs into extent and efficacy.

Robertson marks a new division of Acts opening with Rome on the horizon and notes the change of route; Ellicott argues that the Greek implies communion with the Divine Spirit and supplies the two motives from the letters; Barnes reads the phrase as a mental resolution and notes how Paul reached Rome.
Calvin takes the purpose to be formed by the motion of the Spirit and explains why God conceals the issue from his servants; he also notes Paul giving up Timothy for the Macedonians' sake.
Henry leaves both senses of "in the spirit" open and denies that seeing Rome meant sightseeing.
Clarke dates the departure and assigns the first Corinthian letter to this period; Wesley measures the reach of the plan against Caesar and Alexander.
Chrysostom takes the words to show that all Paul did was not of his own power, and hears him excusing his delay to the Corinthians.

sides.position: the Holy Spirit, moving and governing Paul
Paul's own mind, a resolution not yet made public
either may be meant

schools.summary: Barnes explains why a city treasurer was the right man for a collection; Ellicott lights the mission from the Corinthian letters; Robertson renders the last clause literally, supplies the open door as the motive, and notes that the festival month and the riot cut the stay short.
Gill supposes the two went to give notice of Paul's coming and to prepare for him.
Clarke traces Timothy's further errand and the later notice of Erastus at Corinth.

themes: stayed in Asia for a season

schools.summary: Robertson names the litotes, identifies "the Way" as the movement's title, and notes that trouble had preceded this stir; Barnes and Ellicott gloss the phrase.

Gill reports the versions' renderings; Calvin contrasts the uproar with Paul's hope of a quiet departure, makes covetousness the plague behind it, applies the case to the clergy of his own day, and sets Satan behind Demetrius.
Clarke takes "that way" of the gospel the apostles preached.

Barnes takes the shrines for portable silver temples containing an image; Ellicott identifies the word with the inner sanctuary, traces the temple's history and describes the image as an ugly survival of nature-worship whose very ugliness gave it power; Robertson notes that only terra-cotta shrines survive, reports Ramsay and Zoeckler, and reads Demetrius as the head of a guild.
Clarke describes the temple's dimensions and history and takes the shrines as models of the building; Wesley calls them silver models bought by citizens and strangers alike.
Chrysostom asks how temples could be made of silver, guesses at small boxes, and states that wherever there is idolatry money is at the bottom of it.

sides.position: models of the temple building itself
models of the inner sanctuary with the image inside it
perhaps small boxes
a misunderstanding of the title "temple-warden"

schools.summary: Robertson notes that employer and employees met together, so this was no strike, and reads the appeal as piety for the sake of revenue; Ellicott distinguishes skilled craftsmen from labourers and generalises the element of vested interest, turning it against the later Church as well; Barnes limits "wealth" to a livelihood.
Gill takes the first group for the masters of the trade; Calvin denies the plea any dignity and turns the case on the reader's own self-interest.
Clarke calls the trade most lucrative and gives the word the sense of abundance.
Chrysostom notes that Demetrius was rich and could bear the loss, while the men he roused were poor and said nothing themselves.

themes: by this craft we have our wealth

schools.summary: Barnes calls the speech a heathen's testimony to Paul's success; Ellicott allows for the exaggeration of alarm but confirms it from Pliny, and notes that the mob-leader has committed himself to the view that the idol is the god; Robertson marks the contempt in "this Paul", the present tense of god-making, and the slight to the workmen's craft.
Gill notes the appeal to sight and hearing together.
Clarke reads the sentence as a pleasing account of the apostles' success; Wesley infers that the images were generally believed to hold a real divinity.
Chrysostom observes that the speech nearly argued the other way, since a God who could turn so many deserved a question.

themes: no gods which are made with hands
the idol taken for the god

schools.summary: Barnes notes the order of the two counts and traces the temple's burnings and final ruin; Robertson gives the verb its force of exposure and censure and checks the claim of universal worship against Pausanias; Ellicott notes the goddess's standing epithet, quotes Apuleius, and calls the silversmith an unconscious prophet.
Gill puts the commercial logic in a sentence; Calvin attacks the order of the speech, exposes the plea of religion as a cloak, and names the appeal to numbers as superstition's refuge.
Clarke shows the Ephesian Diana to be a composite nature-goddess, which is why she is called great; Wesley denies that a multitude of those who err turns error into truth.

Ellicott and Robertson read the tense as continuous and identify the cry as the votaries' liturgical shout, attested in inscriptions; Robertson notes the variant without the article and the Codex Bezae addition; Barnes reads the clamour as a tactic for raising a persecution.
Gill notes that masters and workmen were affected alike.

themes: great is Diana of the Ephesians

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph, that the shout answers nothing Demetrius reported Paul as saying, is read off the text by the summary rather than taken from a witness

schools.summary: Robertson describes the flood of confusion and the mob psychology, and gives the theatre's estimated capacity; Ellicott supplies the rumour that spread, compares the panic at Athens, and identifies Gaius and Aristarchus from the later record; Barnes explains the theatre's civic use.
Gill pictures the cry carried through the streets; Calvin reads the crowd as painted in a picture, counsels invincible constancy, and rests on God's hand upon the helm.
Clarke quotes Tacitus and Frontinus on theatres used for public consultation and lays the blame on one unprincipled man; Wesley supposes the mob meant the two men for the beasts.

Robertson reads the imperfect as resistance to pressure and says Paul would not leave his comrades in the lurch; Ellicott catches both the zeal and the friends' fear and connects the scene with the fighting with beasts; Barnes states the purpose soberly.
Gill finds in the attempt the greatness of Paul's soul; Calvin praises the pairing of constancy with modesty, since he yielded to those who knew the case better.
Wesley says he was above all fear and meant to plead his companions' cause.

Barnes and Ellicott and Robertson between them describe the Asiarchs — ten men chosen from the chief cities, annually elected, financing the games themselves; Ellicott dates the festival from the Corinthian letter and notes Paul's standing with men in authority; Robertson reads the imperfect as insistence over Paul's protest.
Gill objects to rendering them princes and cites Philip the Asiarch at Polycarp's martyrdom.
Clarke calls them a sort of high priest, denies they can have been Christians, and wonders whether Paul went in after all; Wesley identifies them as the priests presiding over the games.

debates.question: What were the Asiarchs to Paul?

sides.position: friends who had heard him preach, though nothing shows them converts
certainly not Christians, but genuinely his friends
men who thought highly of him and were at least tolerant of his preaching

schools.summary: Barnes and Robertson admire the description of a mob and read the tenses as continuous and settled; Robertson finds contempt in Luke's use of "assembly" for such a gathering and notes that Demetrius has now vanished from view; Ellicott argues from the vividness for an eyewitness source and notes the particles that carry the reader back into the theatre.
Gill guards against reading the disagreement as one among the disciples.
Henry draws the rule against haste and unchecked passion.
Clarke shows that the word for assembly covers any gathering, lawful or not; Wesley notes that such ignorance is usual in a crowd.

Barnes corrects "his defence" to "a defence" and identifies the aim as clearing the Jews; Ellicott reads the same motive, suggests a trade connection with Demetrius, and paints the failed attempt to gain a hearing; Robertson explains the Jews' fear of a mob turning on them and notes that Alexander never got a word out.
Gill accepts the identification with the coppersmith; Calvin thinks the Jews meant him to be killed and draws a warning about apostasy.
Clarke agrees he was a Jewish advocate and no Christian; Wesley takes him for a Christian pushed forward into danger.

debates.question: Who was Alexander, and whose cause was he to plead?

sides.position: a Jewish spokesman put forward to clear the Jews of blame
a Christian thrust forward by the Jews to expose him to danger
a Jew pushed out so that the crowd might kill him

schools.summary: Robertson and Ellicott give the verb its force of full recognition, and Robertson notes the broken construction and the unanimity that argument had failed to produce; Barnes explains the ancient hour and the two purposes the shouting served.
Gill puts the crowd's reasoning in a sentence; Calvin weighs the shout as a hollow confession and turns the comparison against sluggish believers.
Wesley notes that they prevented him as an enemy of images.

themes: when they knew he was a Jew

schools.summary: Robertson describes the recorder as the chief magistrate of a free city and notes that he waited for the noise to exhaust itself; Ellicott calls him the keeper of the records, weighs his caution against Demetrius' frankness, and names him the Gamaliel of Ephesus; Barnes explains "temple-keeper" as an office of honour and marks the confidence that history refuted.
Gill objects to the small English title; Calvin refuses to admire the speech, since the tumult was quieted at the price of maintaining the worship, and notes why Luke recorded that Paul was kept out.
Clarke traces the history of the title and passes on Isidore's account of artists killed to hide an image's making; Wesley detects a purpose in the appeal to a heaven-fallen image.

themes: quieting a crowd at a price

schools.summary: Robertson notes the rare verbal adjective and observes what is being called undeniable; Barnes lays out the syllogism; Ellicott hears an official acceptance of the cult rather than devotion, and a worldly prudence in the counsel against zeal.
Gill reads the sentence as reassurance that the crowd had mistaken the men.
Henry turns the advice into a rule for private and public affairs alike.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph, that the counsel is good whatever the creed of the man giving it, is the summary's own; Ellicott supplies the judgement that the devotion was official rather than personal

schools.summary: Barnes corrects "churches" to temples and draws the lesson that reason, not reviling, is the way to remove an evil; Ellicott notes the inscriptions naming sacrilege as a capital crime and contrasts the apostles' manner with Alexander's; Robertson explains how gravely temple-robbing was viewed and calls the seizure rash.
Gill identifies the two men; Calvin accepts the acquittal but rejects the recorder's definition of sacrilege, since transferring God's honour to idols is the real thing.
Clarke commends the choice of an incontrovertible fact and describes the apostles' method as enlightening the multitude.

themes: neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott explain the court days and the technical force of "implead"; Ellicott accounts for the plural by the joint authority after Silanus' murder; Robertson calls it a rhetorical plural, notes the Trajanic inscription with the same vocabulary, and reads the appeal as a rebuke to lynch-law.
Gill names the ringleaders; Calvin distinguishes private suits from public business and explains the plural by legates keeping court.
Clarke takes the phrase for the terms of law or the sitting of the judges; Wesley says there was one proconsul in every province.

debates.question: Why "deputies" in the plural, when Asia had one proconsul?

sides.position: a rhetorical or general plural
legates who sometimes held court in the proconsul's place
two procurators exercising joint proconsular authority after the murder of Junius Silanus

schools.summary: Barnes distinguishes private wrong from public affairs and derives the word for assembly as that which is called out; Ellicott makes the point legislative rather than judicial and cites an Ephesian inscription using the same phrase; Robertson quotes another and notes that only the Roman authorities could sanction such a meeting.
Gill defines the other matters as anything beyond the trade of Demetrius and the artificers.
Clarke denies that such business belongs to a mob; Wesley describes a body competent to judge religious and political affairs.

fidelity.note: the closing paragraph, describing the recorder as sorting a religious emergency into two ordinary categories, is the summary's framing of what Barnes, Ellicott and Gill each say of one part

schools.summary: Barnes quotes the Roman law making riot a capital offence; Ellicott catches the inclusive "we", notes that the same verb was used of impleading, and produces a Trajanic inscription carrying nearly all the speech's technical terms; Robertson cites Seneca on Roman jealousy of tumultuous meetings.
Gill lists the authorities to whom the city was answerable.
Clarke turns the law against Demetrius, whose life now lay at the mercy of the men he accused; Wesley notes the inoffensive name given to the concourse.

Robertson explains what the formal dismissal accomplished legally and argues from the vividness of the account for an eyewitness source in Aristarchus; Barnes notes the word usually rendered church applied to a riotous assemblage.
Gill marks that the dismissal followed the speech and its arguments.

Clarke calls it another proof that the word covers any assembly, and closes with reflections on the power of right words, the blessing of civil law, and gain as the root of most outcry against reformation.
Cyril of Jerusalem builds a point of catechesis on this very verse, that since the word is used of a mob in a theatre one must ask not merely for the Church but for the catholic Church.
